purpose: Scope boundaries for material intake: what the authors' statements require, where counting of independent cores stops, which parts the authors leave unexpanded or open, and literal source-notation points. No correctness verdict is issued here; each item is a location plus the literal phenomenon.
notation_convention_in_this_file: TeX commands are described without backslash prefixes (for example Lambda, sigma_mu, kappa, mathfrak f, overline X^h). The authoritative literal forms are in the native file at the cited lines.

space: X separable geodesic Gromov-hyperbolic metric space with basepoint o in X; separability is used for compact metrizability of the horofunction compactification (lines 301-310)
G = Isom(X); Busemann cocycle sigma(g,x) = h(g^{-1}o) on the horofunction compactification, with sigma(g,o) = kappa(g) and |sigma(g,x)| <= kappa(g) (line 306)
measure: mu is a probability measure on G, countably supported (line 108)
mu is non-elementary: the semigroup generated by supp mu contains at least two independent loxodromic elements (line 299)
finite exponential moment: some alpha > 0 with integral of exp(alpha d(g.o,o)) dmu(g) finite. This is the hypothesis of Theorem 1.1, Theorem 4.1, Corollary 3.9 and Corollary 1.3

finite second moment (integral of kappa(g)^2 dmu(g) finite) is a separate hypothesis, used by Lemma 3.1, Proposition 3.3, Lemma 3.6 and Lemma 3.8; Proposition 3.4 assumes only that phi is bounded measurable
finite first moment appears only as discussion (LLN and the closing remarks); it is not a hypothesis of any proved result here
statement_domain: Theorem 1.1: Lambda is the limit Laplace transform of (1/n) d(z_n,o) as defined in (1.5); conclusion is a two-sided limit lambda -> 0 of (Lambda(lambda) - lambda l_mu)/lambda^2
Theorem 4.1: for every x in the horofunction compactification both Lambda_x^+ (limsup) and Lambda_x^- (liminf) satisfy the same limit; for x in X they coincide with Lambda (line 733)
Proposition 4.2: only a lower bound, stated for lambda -> 0 (both signs handled, the negative side by replacing M_x with -M_x, lines 811-813)
Proposition 4.3: only an upper bound, stated for lambda -> 0
Proposition 4.4: upper bound with the possibly larger constant v(mu) instead of sigma_mu^2, valid for |lambda| < v(mu)/b with b depending on mu and epsilon

quantifier_and_regularity_notes: Theorem 4.1 quantifies over every x in the horofunction compactification and over both the liminf and limsup transforms, so the statement is a genuine two-sided equality of limits, not a convergence of Lambda itself along all sequences

Proposition 3.3 statement writes sup over x in X (line 434) whereas the surrounding reduction and its uses work with x in the horofunction compactification; the literal supremum range in the printed statement is X. Recorded as a source point, not adjusted
Lemma 3.8 constant C and rate beta are uniform in k and in x in the compactification; the lemma is stated for k in N and any R > 0
Corollary 3.9 iterates limits in the order a -> +infinity outside and lambda -> 0+ inside; the inner n -> +infinity limsup is inside both
Proposition 4.3 proof takes the limit order n -> infinity, then lambda -> 0, then epsilon -> 0 before invoking acceleration (line 886)

The parameter v(mu) is defined as a supremum over the compactification (line 824) and is not known a priori to equal sigma_mu^2; the equality is recovered only in the limit v(mu^{*k})/k -> sigma_mu^2 (4.5)
normalisation_and_limits: The expansion is normalised by lambda^2, not by |lambda|^2 or by a variance; the constant on the Laplace side is sigma_mu^2/2 and on the rate-function side 1/(2 sigma_mu^2)
Lambda(0) = 0 and the first derivative at 0 equals the drift l_mu; the latter is quoted from BMSS Theorem 1.1 and Lemma C.2 (line 142) and is not re-proved
The variance sigma_mu^2 is defined by a double integral against any stationary nu (1.6 and 3.10); independence of nu is proved in Lemma 3.6, so any stationary measure may be used
Time scaling: the random walk uses L_n = X_n ... X_1 and z_n = L_n . o; the paper notes at line 178 that the right random walk has the same law, so the results transfer without change
The acceleration step uses mu^{*k} with Lambda(mu^{*k}) = k Lambda(mu) (line 895) and drift l_{mu^{*k}} = k l_mu implicitly; the limit is taken as k -> infinity
core_counting_boundaries: One core only: the second-order expansion. Proposition 2.2 (submartingale transform) is a construction inside that core, used for the lower bound; it is not counted separately although it is the paper's most general new lemma
Lemma 3.1 is a cited decomposition (BQ, horbez, aoun-sert); it is context plus a verification, not an author-new core
Proposition 3.4 is an adaptation of Benoist--Quint Proposition 3.1 with the continuity hypothesis relaxed to uniform Cesaro convergence; it is a tool for one step, not an independent core
Lemma 3.6, Lemma 3.8, Corollary 3.9 and Proposition 3.3 are quantitative supporting estimates for the same core; Proposition 3.3 is the one consumed by the lower bound through Corollary 3.9
Lemma 4.5 and Proposition 4.4 form the upper-bound mechanism; Proposition 4.3 adds the acceleration step that replaces v(mu) by sigma_mu^2. These are not severable from the core
Corollary 1.3 is a direct application through convex duality and Varadhan's lemma; it does not add a new H2/H3 core
No independent H2/H3 core exists outside this one: the remaining numbered items are a quoted external proposition, remarks, and two open questions
